title: Eleri Button and the Sleepy Moon Smudge
markdown:
Eleri Button cleaned windows at the Grand Treetop Hotel, near enough to the Whispering Peaks that morning mist sometimes signed the upper panes first. She left the glass streak-free enough to make a weasel proud. Meticulous was the kind word. Between the squeegee and the cloth in her miniature tweed waistcoat lived a leather notebook that was not for appointments. It was for suspiciously small mysteries, the sort other people called crumbs and walked past.

She had logged The Case of the Missing Marmalade Seed, which vanished for days and turned up in Mrs. Higgins' teacup, still orange, still accused of nothing. Then The Incident of the Unaccountably Uneven Biscuit Stack, solved by a squirrel with ambition, no shame, and a very particular idea of fairness. Today's entry, written faster than she liked, paw less steady than a professional squeegee permits, read: Baroness’s Favourite Window — Smudge, Unknown Origin, Approx. 1cm, Lunchtime Threat Level: Critical.

The Baroness Von Strudel's bay window looked over a rose garden trimmed to an inch of its life. Eleri had just finished it when a dandelion seed, smaller than a flea, landed with the precision of someone who had practised. She flicked. The seed smeared. A perfect, tiny, infuriating grey thumbprint sat on the glass as if a gnome had signed it. Lunch was in one hour. Her whiskers took the news personally.

Ivy the giraffe came along the grand corridor, neck first, voice like summer leaves. "Eleri, dear. You seem rather energetic. Is everything quite all right?"

Eleri nearly dropped the polish. "Ivy. Just admiring the view. Tremendous view. Very important part of the job. Scenery." She arranged her weasel bulk in front of the mark.

Ivy's large soft eyes blinked. She tilted. "It looks rather as if you are trying to buff out a very small, very determined speck that is enjoying its perch."

Professional pride does not admit defeat to a speck. "Nonsense. A spirited polishing technique. Keeps the glass on its toes. Prevents complacency." She rubbed. The smudge grew more itself, a grey moon that refused to clock out.

A small figure left a velvet armchair. Lily, a guest of about eight, held a well-loved teddy named Bartholomew. She had the habit of seeing what adults had already decided not to. She trotted to the glass until her nose almost touched.

"Excuse me, mister weasel. What's that funny grey mark? It looks like a little cloud that forgot to float away."

"Miss weasel," Ivy said, kind as a correction can be.

Eleri froze. Fur prickled. She could have offered atmosphere, dust, a lecture with diagrams. Lily's gaze did not blink. The manuals, Eleri thought, never mentioned this tool.

She swallowed. "Well, Lily. That's my mistake. I was cleaning, and a tiny bit got smudged. A very small mystery."

Ivy's nod was an anchor. Lily furrowed, then grinned, then giggled.

"It looks like a little sleepy moon. Can I tell the Baroness a sleepy moon is on her window?"

Eleri's heart performed an unprofessional flip. The Baroness. The notebook felt heavier than leather. Stern displeasure had a temperature. Then there was Lily's smile, and Ivy not leaving.

She straightened her tiny spectacles. "Yes, Lily. You can tell her. And I will tell her myself. This smudge is a reminder that even a determined cleaner can make a charmingly imperfect mark."

They walked the corridor together, giraffe shadow and weasel step, past ferns that had never been smudged in their lives. At the suite Eleri took a breath that had to do for courage and explained: the seed, the flick, the threat level in the book, which she opened because hiding it now would have been a second smudge. The Baroness listened with the stillness of someone who has heard worse emergencies involving soup. Eleri waited for wages to shrink.

The Baroness had kinder eyes than rumour allowed, and a fondness for the unexpected that the hotel staff mentioned only after hours. She adjusted her monocle and leaned in until the sleepy moon had a proper audience.

"A sleepy moon, you say? My dear Eleri, I do believe you have discovered a rather delightful form of window art. Whimsical." The smile widened. "And your honesty is worth more than a perfectly clear pane. We are quite proud of the sleepy moon. Prouder of the explanation."

Warmth arrived that polish had never managed. Ivy nudged her, silent. The smudge stayed: a quiet mark, a larger telling. Later, in the notebook, Eleri wrote it down with a sigh that was almost content, and did not raise the threat level. It was, she decided, the most heartwarming mystery she had solved, and the only one that asked to remain on the glass.
characters: Eleri Button (determined weasel window cleaner), Ivy (giraffe friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
